newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgaria crisis hits aspirations of young.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgaria crisis hits aspirations of young.

text.p: The basement of Bulgaria's National Library is the unlikely site of one of Sofia's most fashionable bars, the Biblioteka nightclub.

Waiters wear white shirts and red scarves that mock the past -- to millions of people in former communist eastern Europe the uniform is a reminder of their childhood, when they were members of their countries' Young Communist Leagues.
Ten years ago, Dimi Yekimov, singer in the rock band playing at Biblioteka, also wore a red scarf. Now he wears a t-shirt instead of a white doctor's coat.
Dimi, 27, graduated from the Sofia Medical Academy two years ago but at the moment his only connection to the medical profession is his diploma.
MORE MONEY IN SINGING THAN SURGERY

Like businesses and households nationwide, the hospitals and clinics in Bulgaria have been crippled by the country's economic plight. Reliant on subsidies from a near-bankrupt state, hospitals are turning patients away because funds have dried up in the depths of economic crisis.
Patients must bring their own bedsheets and buy their own food, and poorly paid medical staff lack ordinary equipment. The average doctor's salary is worth less than $30 a month.
Dimi performs in the Biblioteka club every second night, earning more than a chief doctor in a big hospital.

And at the moment, he spends his afternoons outside the gold-domed Alexander Nevski Cathedral with tens of thousands of others, at daily rallies to protest against the rule of the ex-communist Bulgarian Socialist Party.
"I go to the rally every day. I want to say no to the government which for the past several years has ruined my country and stole what was left it after decades of communist rule," Dimi said.
"They turned Bulgarian people into beggars and we cannot let them go on unpunished."
PEOPLE POWER VERSUS SOCIALIST PARTY
The Socialist party, largely composed of ex-communists, has led seven of the eight governments since the end of one-party rule in 1989.

Corruption and delays to economic reforms have produced annual inflation running at more than 300 percent and a flight into dollars has depressed the lev currency to lows around 700 to the dollar now from 70 a year ago.
Bulgarians are still waiting to see the benefits of reforms which transformed the economies of countries like Poland and Hungary.

After months of criticism, Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21 and the opposition does not want the Socialists to complete the almost two years which are left of their parliamentary term.
Daily rallies to demand a general election began on January 6, inspired by weeks of protests aginst the Socialist government in Belgrade.
"Many people who have talent and knowledge, not only doctors but other professions as well, work in other jobs like driving taxis," Dimi said.
"It is not a problem for an architect to become a good plumber but it is a big problem when an architect's talent and education is wasted because he can make more as a plumber."
FAMILY WOES MAY WORSEN
The problem may soon become a family one when Dimi's sister, 22-year-old Rusana, graduates in two years' time from Sofia University where she studies architecture.
She is afraid that she will not be able to find work in the present climate and that, even if she does, she will not be able to support herself on the money she makes.
"I think that there are a lot of people who are angry at the situation but they are too depressed to take action, they have no hope," she said.
Many young Bulgarians, frustrated that they cannot use their qualifications, try to move to richer countries in the hope of a better life.
"There is absolute confusion about our future lives here," said Rusana, who attends the daily rallies with her brother.
"We prefer to stay here but it's getting harder and harder. This doesn't feel like our own country any more, but we're trying to save things, to make things better if we can."
Until now, the only way Dimi and Rusana could express their frustration was to teach their four-year-old dog Jazz to bark furiously whenever he hears the word "communists".
Now they can join tens of thousands of Bulgarians at the rallies and hope their pressure will change things for the better.
